title: the Yoga Vasistha (selections)
hook: two rams lock horns: yesterday's effort and today's
tomorrow: four guards stand at one gate. which one do you befriend first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Yoga Vasistha opened on a prince with no appetite for the world, and a court that took his questions seriously. Today, his teacher's first answer.

Birth charts, fortune cookies, the 'it was meant to be' at the end of a wedding toast: the idea that a life is already written turns up everywhere. Rama has just told the court that the world's prizes come and go on their own. A teacher could leave him there, with everything out of his hands. Vasistha doesn't. He draws a picture instead: two rams with their horns locked in a field, and the stronger one pushing the other back.
screen: `IT WAS MEANT TO BE.` → `IS A LIFE ALREADY WRITTEN?` → `TWO RAMS, HORNS LOCKED.`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit words are paurusha, a person's own effort, and daiva, fate. Vasistha's move is bold. What people call fate, he says, isn't a separate power writing the story from outside. It's the fruit of a person's own earlier effort, coming back around. So when a life feels fixed, that's yesterday's effort pushing. Today's effort is the other ram, and the stronger one wins the field. The effort he praises isn't raw willpower; it's guided by scripture and good teachers. A Christian neighbor would recognize part of this. Paul writes to the Galatians: 'whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.' What you do comes back to you. That much the two share. The honest difference is in the field itself. For Paul, the sowing happens before God, and the harvest he hopes for is life everlasting, reaped from the Spirit. For Vasistha, fate is a person's own past actions, and present effort can overcome them. Both say what you do matters. They say it inside two different pictures of the world. Vasistha's point to Rama is plain: sitting still and waiting on fate gets nothing done.
screen: `PAURUSHA: YOUR OWN EFFORT.` · `FATE IS YESTERDAY'S EFFORT.` · `PAUL: WHAT YOU SOW, YOU REAP.` · `TWO PICTURES OF THE FIELD.` · then, large: `TODAY'S RAM CAN PUSH BACK.`

segments.voice: Plant both feet flat on the floor and press your palms together in front of your chest, gently, so each hand pushes against the other. Feel the two pushes meet and hold. Then soften the pressure, keep your feet planted, and breathe with that steady, ready feeling.
The Yoga Vasistha: here, paurusha against daiva, today's effort against yesterday's, two rams in one field.
For the road: the Yoga Vasistha, in selections, where fate is yesterday's effort and today's can push back. Day sixteen-oh-two.

chat.meaning: Paul and Vasistha share sowing and reaping. In Galatians the harvest is from God; in the Yoga Vasistha, fate is one's own past effort, which present effort can overcome.

notes: Yoga Vasistha run, day 2. Angle: self-effort and fate. 1595 (Kama Sutra) answered a fate objection by calling effort the means; this day takes the Yoga Vasistha's sharper claim that fate IS one's own past effort. Different angle, same theme: check the pair reads well together.
